section_summary: This section completes a consular analysis of the South Manchuria Railway Company’s 1933–34 finances and contains the company’s balance sheet, followed by reports on a proposed new station at Dairen and a detailed review of the company’s 1934–35 accounts, subsidiaries, traffic, mines, ports, and investment program. The later documents concern the forced resignation of railway president Count Hirotaro Hayashi and the appointment of Yosuke Matsuoka, interpreted as preparation for closer cooperation with the Kwantung Army and expanded Japanese economic penetration of North China. Departmental memoranda, statistical enclosures, a newspaper clipping, and financial statements accompany the principal diplomatic despatches.

people.name: John Carter Vincent
people.role: American Consul and author of the concluding 1933–34 financial analysis

people.name: Yosuke Matsuoka
people.role: New president of the South Manchuria Railway; former diplomat, railway vice-president, Diet member, and Japanese delegate to the League of Nations

people.name: Hirotaro Hayashi
people.role: Count and outgoing president of the South Manchuria Railway

people.name: Yoshiaki Hatta
people.role: Vice-president of the South Manchuria Railway and liaison with the Kwantung Army

people.name: Jiro Minami
people.role: General, commander of the Kwantung Army, and Japanese Ambassador to Manchukuo

people.name: Jotaro Yamamoto
people.role: Former president of the South Manchuria Railway and proposed member of Matsuoka’s advisory group

people.name: Araki
people.role: Japanese general cited as a proponent of nationalist idealism

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at the American Embassy in Tokyo

people.name: Naoto Kobiyama
people.role: Managing director of the Pig Iron Joint Sales Company and Showa Coal Company; reported prospective railway vice-president

people.role: President of the Nisso Oil Company, former president of Kawasaki Dockyard Company, and proposed senior railway adviser

subfiles.title: Financial condition and 1933–34 results of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.about: Continuation of a consular analysis of the South Manchuria Railway Company’s balance sheet, operating accounts, and investment policy for fiscal 1933–34.
subfiles.summary: The despatch examines railway, hotel, harbor, colliery, shale-oil, iron, local-administration, and interest accounts, questioning the allocation of unusually large profits to railway operations and costs to the Fushun collieries. It describes the transfer of the Anshan iron properties to Showa Steel Works and the use of Japanese government support and naval purchasing to sustain other enterprises. The conclusion emphasizes the company’s post-1931 shift from directly held assets toward loans, subsidiaries, and construction advances for Manchukuo railways, whose strategic value was unlikely to produce an adequate financial return.

subfiles.title: General Balance Sheet for the Year Ended March 31, 1934
subfiles.about: Official balance sheet and profit-and-loss statement for the South Manchuria Railway Company’s fiscal year ending March 31, 1934.
subfiles.summary: The statement tabulates fixed assets, investments, current assets, construction advances, capital, bonds, deposits, and other liabilities totaling approximately ¥1.613 billion. Its profit-and-loss account reports particularly large railway earnings, smaller profits from hotels, harbors, collieries, and oil distillation, and losses for local administration, general expenses, interest, and depreciation. It also records the allocation of net profit to reserves, dividends, official bonuses, and the carried-forward balance.

subfiles.title: Plans for the Construction of a New South Manchuria Railroad Station at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Report on plans, facilities, contracting, and possible American trade opportunities associated with a new railway station at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The proposed three-story station was designed as the largest and most modern in Manchuria, with separate arrival and departure levels, offices, communications facilities, public amenities, and a roof garden. Its scale reflected expectations that Dairen would continue growing despite Japanese development of the ports of Rashin and Seishin. The consul anticipated a local construction contract, possibly for Fukusho Company, but promised to report any later opportunity for American suppliers.

subfiles.title: Dairen’s New Station
subfiles.about: Illustrated newspaper notice showing the projected new railway station at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reproduces an artist’s rendering of what it describes as the grandest railway station in Manchuria. Its caption states that the building was expected to be completed by the end of the following year.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on the South Manchuria Railway balance sheet for fiscal 1934–35
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Internal summary of the principal findings in the July 8, 1935 Dairen despatch on the railway company’s accounts.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes increases in total assets, fixed property, investments, loans to Manchukuo State Railways, traffic, coal output, and harbor profits, alongside declining shale-oil profits. It also highlights the proposed 1935–36 budget, Cabinet-approved expenditures for new enterprises, and the reported arrival of 15,000 new company employees in Manchuria. It concludes that no departmental action was required.

subfiles.title: Comments on the Balance Sheet of the South Manchuria Railway Company for the Fiscal Year, 1934–35
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Detailed consular analysis of the South Manchuria Railway Company’s financial position, operating enterprises, and forthcoming budget.
subfiles.summary: The despatch reports assets of approximately ¥1.811 billion, major increases in investments and bonds, and continuing advances and unpaid interest associated with Manchukuo State Railways. It compares six years of railway traffic, coal production, port operations, and enterprise profits, while warning that accounting figures were likely manipulated for military and policy purposes. Separate discussions cover hotels, Dairen and Rashin harbor works, the Fushun and Yantai collieries, shale-oil production, Showa Steel Works, civic institutions, interest costs, and profit distribution. The proposed 1935–36 program emphasized railways, ports, mining, schools, hospitals, and other Cabinet-approved enterprises.

subfiles.title: Table I — South Manchuria Railway Company Affiliated Concerns Established in 1934
subfiles.about: List of eight affiliated companies organized in 1934 with their capitalization and establishment dates.
subfiles.summary: The table identifies new concerns in petroleum, automobiles, cotton, coal, gold, cement, soybeans, and electricity. Their stated authorized capital illustrates the breadth of the railway company’s expanding industrial affiliations, although the accompanying despatch cautions that the company’s actual share of each investment was often unclear.

subfiles.title: Table II — Expenditures and Income of South Manchuria Railway Company Enterprises for the Fiscal Years 1929–1935
subfiles.about: Comparative table of income and expenditures by enterprise from 1929–30 through 1934–35, with estimates for 1935–36.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure compares railway, hotel, harbor, colliery, oil, ironworks, administrative, interest, general, depreciation, and net-profit accounts over six completed fiscal years. It shows the growing dominance of railway revenues, fluctuating industrial results, and persistent losses in local administration and several overhead categories. A final column supplies the company’s projected income and expenditure for 1935–36.

subfiles.title: General Balance Sheet for the Year Ending March 31, 1935
subfiles.about: Official South Manchuria Railway Company balance sheet and profit-and-loss account for fiscal 1934–35.
subfiles.summary: The statement presents assets and liabilities totaling approximately ¥1.811 billion, including fixed property, investments, current assets, construction advances, capital stock, reserves, bonds, deposits, and unadjusted accounts. The profit-and-loss account records a net annual profit of roughly ¥46.5 million after depreciation, with the largest operating profit coming from railways. The disposition statement allocates the accumulated profit to reserves, government and public dividends, bonuses, and a carried-forward balance.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on the appointment of Yosuke Matsuoka
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Internal synopsis of the Tokyo Embassy’s analysis of Matsuoka’s appointment as president of the South Manchuria Railway.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reviews Matsuoka’s prominence as Japan’s delegate during the League of Nations debate over Manchuria and identifies him as an extreme nationalist popular with the Army and patriotic societies. It contrasts him with Count Hayashi, who had resisted military plans and further overseas investment. The appointment is interpreted as a move to ensure railway cooperation with the Kwantung Army’s projected economic program in North China.

subfiles.title: The Appointment of Mr. Yosuke Matsuoka as President of the South Manchuria Railway
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Embassy analysis of the political, military, and economic significance of Matsuoka’s appointment as railway president.
subfiles.summary: The despatch attributes Count Hayashi’s resignation to disagreements with the Kwantung Army, General Minami, railway vice-president Hatta, and Finance Minister Takahashi. It reviews Matsuoka’s diplomatic and political career and argues that his appointment was intended to align the company with military plans for economic penetration of North China. Japanese press commentary depicts the railway as resuming its role as Japan’s politico-economic advance guard, while financiers fear the enormous capital requirements and potential risks. Matsuoka publicly advocated concentrating on agriculture, forestry, mining, cotton, and the purchasing power of Manchurian farmers rather than indiscriminate industrialization.

subfiles.title: Departmental memorandum on problems confronting the new South Manchuria Railway president
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Internal summary of the Dairen consulate’s August 8 report on Matsuoka’s plans and the railway company’s financial problems.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Hayashi was apparently forced out because he could not cooperate with the Kwantung Army and General Minami. It summarizes Matsuoka’s reported plans for an advisory brain trust, agricultural and cotton development, profitable railway operation, review of North China activities and subsidiaries, and avoidance of political questions. It also notes anxiety among Japanese financial leaders over the roughly ¥600 million invested in Manchukuo since the 1931 incident.

subfiles.title: Problems Confronting the New President of the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Confidential survey of the circumstances of Hayashi’s removal and the prospective policies, personnel, and financial program of Matsuoka’s administration.
subfiles.summary: Drawing largely on Japanese and Manchurian newspapers, the despatch argues that Hayashi’s abrupt resignation demonstrated the military’s influence and resulted from his opposition to railway reorganization and disagreement over North China investment. It discusses the possible replacement of Hatta by Naoto Kobiyama, the proposed appointment of Kojiro Matsukata as chief economic adviser, the need for additional capital, and General Minami’s insistence that the company remain subject to official control. Matsuoka is reported to be organizing a brain trust and advocating agricultural development, cotton and wool production, safer investment conditions, and renewed examination of the company’s North China and subsidiary operations. The document continues beyond page 156.
